use when the evidence is a virtual disk, a split set, a volume manager's member, an encrypted volume or has snapshots.
not for offset arithmetic once the volume is found (evidence/imaging) or telling encryption from damage (filesystem/encrypted).
an offset means something only inside one address space.

walk the layers in order and note which one each number belongs to: container, backing chain, device set, partition table, encryption, mapping layer (lvm, dynamic disk, storage space, raid), file system, snapshot.
container. file_type and image_layout name it from its first bytes (a candidate, not a validation);
file_type also says whether they agree with the extension, only a claim by whoever named the file:
raw, dd, .img, .001 the bytes of a disk or volume
e01, ex01, l01 encase: compressed, with an acquisition record; physical, volume or (l01) logical
vhd, vhdx, vmdk, qcow2 a virtual disk with its own header, possibly a backing chain and snapshots
ad1 ftk imager's logical image: files, no volume (evidence/ad1)
a directory or a zip a collection, not an image (evidence/collections)
inventory every segment, descriptor, extent and backing file before parsing; record the state you read.
a split e01 is one image: give the first segment.
a split raw set is not: give the sleuth kit every segment in order (the first alone ends early);
image_layout reads one path, or the descriptor.
virtual disks. qemu-img info --backing-chain shows the chain and the snapshots (plain info only the immediate backing file).
when mmls and fsstat open the container, their offsets are sectors of the virtual disk.
convert (qemu-img convert -o raw) only when the next tool cannot open it, to a separate output, and record the state chosen, the options and the output's size and digest.
img_stat prints size and format as the sleuth kit reads it, the bound for any scan over all of it;
mapping layers. mmls names the slot but fsstat cannot read it: the file system starts inside a logical volume whose metadata is at the front of the member.
rebuild it from that metadata and all the members with a reader that supports the layer:

target-query (dissect; it also opens e01, vmdk, qcow and a collection behind one interface, with a plugin per artefact family) or the linux pack's filesystem/storage when loaded; check the version the image carries.
a signature inside a member is a candidate, not the extent mapping.
validate the geometry, the metadata's consistency and that files read before accepting the volume.
a missing member is a limitation.
apfs. fsapfsinfo reads a container's structure; snapshots, fusion drives and t2-based encryption are not supported, so a failure there is the reader's limit.
whether the sleuth kit reads apfs is a fact of its build: try fsstat, record mmls -v (filesystem/apfs, macos pack, when loaded).
a snapshot, shadow copy or earlier backing layer is a separate source with its own time: say which state each result is.
record. each layer passed, its identity, the tool and version, the offset in its own units, the sector size, what was missing.
does not show. that an unread layer holds nothing, or that a reconstructed volume is the one the system used.
use when a .db, .sqlite or an app store is the evidence.
not for other database kinds or for recovering deleted records.

the set. a database is the main file plus a -wal (committed changes the main file may not hold yet, older pages, an incomplete transaction), a -shm (an index of the wal) and a -journal (a rollback journal, hot when a write was interrupted).
from an image, extract each file beside the database (filesystem/extract) into one directory under the main file's name plus the suffix.
a copy of the main file alone is a different state; a live set copied file by file may not be one state.
snapshot, then query. sqlite_query opens the file it is given read-only and immutable, so a wal beside it is reported (snapshot_status:
wal not applied) and not read.

run sqlite_snapshot on the main file as a job: it copies the set into original/ with sha256s (and says changed_during_copy if a live file moved), reads the wal against the format, and has sqlite apply it in applied/database.sqlite.
give sqlite_query the snapshot directory or its database.

read the receipt. wal.frames_committed (applied) against frames_uncommitted_valid (valid frames after the last commit: never applied), first_invalid_frame (a leftover of an earlier generation is normal; a checksum mismatch or a file ending inside a frame is damage: the snapshot is partial), counts_agree (sqlite and the tool found the same number of committed frames), rollback_journal (copied, never rolled back: the main file may hold an interrupted write), applied.pages_of_the_main_file_changed_by_the_wal.
query. read the schema first (sqlite_master; pragmas user_version, application_id, freelist_count), then ask.
values are typed: a blob is length, sha256 and blob_b64 (short) or blob_b64_head, its first head_bytes (long); text that is not utf-8 keeps its bytes.
the whole result is in rows_file; an inline page is not the result.
time columns have a unit and an epoch the schema or the app decides, not the value's look (timeline/clocks).
an app's schema changes between versions: take a column's meaning from the version the evidence carries.
record. the state a result is (as acquired, or wal applied), the receipt, the database's sha256, the query, the rows_file, and the table, rowid and column of each value cited.
does not show. a snapshot and a query show the rows sqlite holds.
they do not recover deleted records, the freelist or unallocated pages (a non-zero freelist_count says free pages exist, not what they held), and a row's absence is not the event's absence.
of a database encrypted by an extension (sqlcipher) the tool shows only the first bytes and their entropy, which identify nothing.
rows of cookie, login, token, key and message tables hold secrets and private text: run the query as a job with secret_output: true
and cite table, row locator and column, never the value
never the value, a fragment of it, or the sha256 and base64 of a short blob.
limit is 1 or more, so the inline page always carries at least one row of values: on such a table select only locators (rowid, length(col), typeof(col))
use when you turn a stored value into a time, convert a zone, or order events across clocks.
not for choosing parsers for a machine timeline (timeline/super) or for an artefact's field layout (the artefact's own skill).

keep, per timestamp: the raw value, the field name, its encoding, epoch, unit and resolution, its zone semantics (utc, a fixed offset, local time of an unknown zone, none), the source and locator, and what event the field describes (a file's modification is not a person's action).
convert last; keep the raw value beside the result.
epoch. the artefact's schema decides which clock wrote a number, never the reading that looks plausible.

timestamp_decode lists what the number would be under each epoch in common use (unix in four resolutions, filetime, webkit, apple, hfs+, ole, dos), exactly (fractions to the nanosecond, the rest in remainder_s).
it applies no zone or daylight-saving rule (dos and ole carry none).
the plausible range is a ranking aid, not evidence: for an old, sentinel or unusual value keep every reading (the default) and decide from the schema.
utc, offset-bearing and local-without-zone are three kinds of value.
do not convert a value already in utc.
a local time needs the zone and its rule on the event's date, daylight saving included.
find the zone where the artefact family keeps it (the registry on windows;
/etc/localtime and configuration on linux) and record where.
a present-day setting is not proof of a past one, and one host setting does not fit every source.
a repeated local hour (a daylight-saving change) is ambiguous: keep both readings until another source chooses.
a local time in the skipped hour does not exist: it points to a wrong zone, rule or clock; record it as found.
a stamp with no year (traditional syslog) needs a year basis: record the text, the basis and the zone applied.
when utc cannot be established, record the observation and the limit, not a utc time you lack.
resolution and order. seconds (syslog), 2 seconds (dos), 100 ns (filetime), a whole day (a date-only record).
invent no order inside a resolution: sort equal times by a fixed rule and say which.
a logged clock change is a finding; no record of one does not show a steady clock.
correlate independent clocks and carry the offset or drift as an uncertainty.
monotonic time orders events inside the sequence it is defined for (a boot, a journal instance, a retained usn or $logfile range).
do not merge unrelated sequences, and across boots and hosts anchor on independent sources.
ntfs $standard_information and $file_name times are two sets of observations, each changeable by different means.
when they disagree, say so and trust neither as a clock.
a creation later than modification is a lead (copying, extraction, restoration and ordinary file system behaviour explain it).
record. the zone and its source, the year basis, why the schema fixes the epoch, the uncertainty, what would disprove the reading.
does not show. a timestamp shows what a clock the artefact trusted wrote into that field, not when a person acted, that two clocks agree, or that a time order is causal.
